commitResults.messageTitle: Add ASCII banner to Cole's greeting and reorganize Task/Event/ToDo/Deadline classes
Add ColeException class for custom error handling
Handle invalid and incomplete commands with ColeException (Level 5)

commitResults.messageBody:
Apply the Java coding standard to all classes in the cole package:
- Add the missing space between ) and { in method and constructor headers
- Move else/else-if branches onto the same line as the closing brace
- Rename the divider constant to DIVIDER to follow the constant
  naming convention
- Normalise spacing in the ColeException class declaration
- Add the missing newline at the end of ToDo.java

No behaviour changes; all commands produce identical output.

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace magic numbers with named constants
commitResults.messageBody:
The command-parsing code used bare numeric literals (100, 4, 9, 5) whose
meaning was only discoverable by counting characters in the command word.
A reader had to verify by hand that 9 was the right offset for
"deadline ", which is exactly the kind of hidden assumption the code
quality guideline on magic numbers warns about.

Introduce MAX_TASKS for the task array capacity and COMMAND_TODO,
COMMAND_DEADLINE and COMMAND_EVENT for the command words, then derive the
substring offsets from the constants instead of hard-coding them.

Deriving the offsets exposed a latent inconsistency: the deadline branch
used substring(9) to skip both the command word and the following space,
while todo and event used the command length and trimmed afterwards. The
deadline description is now trimmed too, so all three branches parse the
same way and the offsets no longer depend on an off-by-one convention
that differs per command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename identifiers to describe what they actually hold or do
commitResults.messageBody:
Several names did not match the thing they named, which forces a reader
to reconstruct the meaning from surrounding code:

- 'actions' held Task objects, not actions. Renamed to 'tasks' so the
  array name matches its element type.
- 'taskCounts' is a single count, not a collection of counts. Renamed to
  'taskCount'.
- 'markedSymbol' is a noun phrase but the method is an accessor that
  returns the status icon. Renamed to 'getStatusIcon', which follows the
  guideline that methods are named with verbs.
- 'markAction' and 'unmarkAction' describe the UI command that triggers
  them rather than the effect on the task. Renamed to 'markAsDone' and
  'markAsNotDone', which say what happens to the object.

Names only; no behaviour change.

commitResults.messageTitle: Move console output out of Task
commitResults.messageBody:
Task.markAsDone and markAsNotDone changed the object's state and also
printed a confirmation message to System.out. That mixes two levels of
abstraction in one method: updating a task is a data concern, telling the
user about it is a UI concern. The SLAP guideline asks that a code
fragment stay at a single level of abstraction.

The mixing also made Task unusable outside a console program and hid the
output from the reader of Cole.main, where every other message is
printed. A future 'list' or 'load' operation that needs to mark tasks
without printing had no way to do so.

Task now only changes its own state, and Cole prints the confirmation
next to the divider lines it already prints. Output is unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Remove duplicated message strings and divider printing
commitResults.messageBody:
Two kinds of copy-paste had accumulated, both of which the guideline on
minimising code duplication warns about because every copy is a place the
next edit can be forgotten.

First, three error messages were written out more than once: the event
/from-/to message appeared four times, the event description message
twice, and the 'task number doesn't exist' message twice. Changing the
wording meant finding every copy, and a missed copy would leave the
program giving two different answers to the same mistake. These are now
the constants ERROR_EVENT_TIME, ERROR_EVENT_DESCRIPTION and
ERROR_TASK_NOT_FOUND.

Second, almost every message was printed as the same three-step sequence:
a divider, the message lines, another divider. That shape was written out
nine times, and in the mark and unmark branches the opening divider was
printed before the try block while the closing one was repeated inside
each catch clause, so the pairing was not visible in one place.
printFramed(String...) now owns that shape, which also lets the mark and
unmark branches drop the leading divider and keep the whole message in a
single call.

Output is unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Check the task list capacity with a guard clause
commitResults.messageBody:
addTask filled the array inside a try block and caught
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException to detect that the list was full. Using an
exception as the normal signal for an expected condition is the unsafe
shortcut the guidelines describe: the catch clause is far from the line
that can throw, and it would silently swallow an out-of-bounds error
raised by any other statement that later joins the block, turning a real
bug into a 'list is full' message.

The condition is known before the write, so addTask now tests
taskCount == MAX_TASKS up front and returns early. This also follows the
guideline on making the happy path prominent: the full-list case is
handled and dismissed in three lines at the top, and the normal add is
left un-nested below it rather than buried inside a try block.

Verified at the boundary: the 100th task is still added and the 101st
reports that the list is full.

commitResults.messageTitle: Split main into one handler per command
commitResults.messageBody:
main was about 110 lines and held every level of abstraction at once: the
read-dispatch loop, the substring arithmetic that separates a command
word from its arguments, the /by and /from-/to parsing rules, the
validation of each field, and the printing. That breaks both the
guideline on method length, which asks for under 30 lines, and SLAP,
which asks that one fragment stay at one level of abstraction. Reading
the loop meant scrolling past forty lines of event parsing to find the
next branch.

main is now the dispatch loop only, and each branch delegates to
listTasks, markTask, addTodo, addDeadline or addEvent. Two shared
helpers carry the parsing detail that was repeated inline: isCommand
tests the 'word' / 'word ...' pair that each of the three add commands
matched by hand, and argumentsOf performs the length-checked substring.
Every method is now under 30 lines.

mark and unmark differed only in which Task method they called and in two
message strings, so they share markTask with a boolean, rather than
keeping two near-identical copies.

argumentsOf deliberately does not trim. The deadline and event branches
split the raw argument string on ' /by ' and ' /from ', so a leading
space is significant: trimming it turns 'deadline  /by Sunday' from a
missing-description error into a missing-/by error. Only addTodo, which
already trimmed, trims.

Output is unchanged for all 22 commands in the manual test, including
every malformed-input case.

commitResults.messageTitle: Reduce the visibility of Cole's internals to private
commitResults.messageBody:
Every field and method in Cole was public, including the tasks array and
the taskCount that indexes it. The guideline on minimising the scope of
variables warns against exactly this: a public mutable static array is a
global variable, and any class could write tasks[50] directly or set
taskCount out of step with the array contents, which would break the
capacity check added earlier and silently corrupt the list.

Nothing outside Cole uses any of them. main stays public because the JVM
needs it as the entry point; DIVIDER, tasks, taskCount, printGreetings,
addTask and printError are now private, so the class's surface is the one
method that is genuinely its interface.

Verified that the project still compiles and that output is unchanged.
